lessons.title: Mid and Late Cycle Leaders: Capital Goods, Metals, and Energy

body.text: Mid and late cycle leaders need a mature cycle: full order books, factories near capacity, and commodity prices pushed up by strong demand. The catch is that their best earnings tend to arrive when the cycle is closest to turning.

children.text: Lesson 3.2 covered the sectors that lead out of a downturn. This lesson moves round the clock to the sectors that take over as the expansion matures and heads into its late stage: capital goods and infrastructure, metals and mining, and energy. They share a heavy dependence on investment and commodity cycles, large fixed costs, and a tendency to look cheapest exactly when they are most dangerous.

children.text: Capital Goods and Infrastructure

Capital goods companies build what other companies and governments invest in: power plants, metro lines, refineries, factories, and transmission networks. Their revenue follows the capex cycle, which Lesson 2.2 showed usually gets going once capacity utilisation crosses the 75% to 80% zone. That places them in the middle of the cycle, after the early cycle rebound in consumption has pushed factories close to full.

markDefs.definition: New orders received in a period divided by revenue booked in the same period. Above 1 means the order book is growing faster than the company is executing it, which points to future revenue growth. Below 1 means the backlog is shrinking.

children.text: For investors, the key numbers are the order book, the order inflow each quarter, and how fast orders turn into revenue. Two simple ratios capture them. The
book-to-bill ratio
tells you whether the backlog is growing, and order book cover tells you how many years of revenue are already locked in.

body.caption: Measure inflow and revenue over the same period

body.title: Read the Order Pipeline
body.prompt: A capital goods company received new orders worth ₹8,000 crore in a year and booked revenue of ₹5,000 crore in the same year. What is its book-to-bill ratio?
body.explanation: ₹8,000 crore divided by ₹5,000 crore is 1.6. The company is winning orders 60% faster than it is executing them, so its backlog is growing. If its order book were ₹60,000 crore against trailing revenue of ₹20,000 crore, order book cover would be 3 years. That is revenue visibility, not profit certainty: margins depend on how well contracts are priced and executed.

children.text: Pair those company numbers with the macro data. Real gross fixed capital formation grew 11.9% in April to June 2026, against 5.8% a year earlier. When government capex, private investment, and order books are all rising together, the capex cycle is doing what the mid cycle phase of the clock expects.

body.text: An order book is not the same as profit. Late in the cycle, three things can hurt capital goods companies even with record backlogs: input costs such as steel, copper, and wages rise faster than fixed-price contracts allow; working capital gets stretched when clients, including governments, pay slowly; and execution slows as supply chains and labour tighten. Always check margins and cash flow, not just order inflow.

children.text: Metals and Mining

Metal producers are price takers in a global market. Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Hindalco, and Vedanta cannot set the price of steel or aluminium; they earn the spread between international prices and their own costs. With huge fixed costs in blast furnaces and smelters, small moves in prices produce large moves in profit.

body.caption: Why metal profits swing: a steel producer's EBITDA per tonne (₹, illustrative)

body.title: Metal Price Sensitivity
body.prompt: Using the table, a 10% rise in the realised steel price takes EBITDA per tonne from ₹10,000 to ₹15,500. By what percentage does EBITDA per tonne rise?
body.explanation: ₹15,500 divided by ₹10,000 is 1.55, a rise of 55%. A 10% price move becomes a 55% profit move because costs stay fixed. The same maths works in reverse: a 10% price fall cuts EBITDA per tonne by 55%, to ₹4,500. This is why metal stocks can double in an upswing and halve in a downturn, and why the P/E trap from Lesson 1.3 bites hardest here.

children.text: Metal cycles are driven as much by China as by India. China produces and consumes the majority of the world's steel, and when its domestic demand weakens, its mills export the surplus. In 2024, China's steel exports reached a record 111.1 million tonnes, pressuring prices across Asia. India responded with a safeguard duty on key flat steel imports: 12% from 21 April 2025, stepping down to 11.5% and then 11% over three years.

body.text: For Indian metal stocks, watch three things beyond the Indian cycle: China's property and infrastructure demand, which sets global steel and aluminium prices; the US dollar, since most metals are priced in dollars; and Indian trade policy, such as the steel safeguard duty, which can shield domestic prices from cheap imports.

children.text: Energy: Three Very Different Businesses
The energy sector is where textbook sector rotation most often misleads Indian investors, because "energy" contains businesses that move in opposite directions when crude oil prices change.

children.text: Upstream Producers

ONGC and Oil India earn more on every barrel when crude prices rise, which makes them classic late cycle beneficiaries on the Investment Clock. But in India, the government shares the windfall. When crude spiked in 2022, the government imposed a special additional excise duty, a windfall tax, of ₹23,250 per tonne on domestic crude production from 1 July 2022. It was only scrapped on 2 December 2024, after prices had fallen.
Oil Marketing Companies

IOC, BPCL, and HPCL refine crude and sell petrol, diesel, and LPG. When crude rises and retail prices are held steady, their marketing margins collapse. Between April and September 2022, with petrol and diesel prices frozen, the three companies posted a combined net loss of ₹21,201 crore, even after a one-time ₹22,000 crore government grant for past LPG losses. When crude later fell and retail prices were not cut as quickly, their profits recovered sharply.

columns.label: Upstream producers (ONGC, Oil India)
points: Revenue per barrel rises with crude prices
Tend to benefit late in the cycle and in overheat phases
Upside can be capped by windfall taxes or pricing directions

columns.label: Oil marketing companies (IOC, BPCL, HPCL)
points: Input costs rise while retail fuel prices may be held steady
Marketing margins can turn sharply negative, as in April to September 2022
Often benefit when crude prices fall
Heavily exposed to government pricing decisions

children.text: Power Utilities

NTPC and Power Grid earn largely regulated returns on the capacity they build, which makes their earnings steadier than most cyclicals. They benefit from long-term demand growth and from the capex cycle in generation and transmission. India's peak power demand hit a then record of 250 GW on 30 May 2024, and then a new high of 270.8 GW on 21 May 2026, helped by heatwaves and around 65 GW of capacity added in FY26. That combination of growth and regulated returns is why utilities can hold up well late in the cycle and into a slowdown.
The Late Cycle Trap
These sectors are most dangerous exactly when they look most attractive. Four patterns repeat.
Peak earnings, low P/E. Metal and energy profits are highest when commodity prices peak, so their P/E ratios look cheapest at the top of the cycle.
Capacity arrives late. Capex decisions made in the boom turn into new plants just as demand cools, creating oversupply and falling prices.
Costs catch up. Rising wages, raw materials, and interest costs squeeze margins on fixed-price contracts and highly leveraged balance sheets.
Policy steps in. When commodity profits look excessive or inflation bites, governments impose windfall taxes, freeze retail prices, or change trade duties.

body.title: Go deeper: why commodity cycles overshoot

children.text: Commodity markets overshoot in both directions because supply responds slowly to price.
A new mine, oilfield, or steel plant takes years to build. When prices rise, supply cannot respond quickly, so prices overshoot.
By the time new capacity arrives, demand may already be cooling, so prices then overshoot on the way down.
Inventories amplify the swing: buyers stock up when prices rise and destock when they fall.
A stronger US dollar tends to weigh on dollar-priced commodities, while a weaker dollar supports them.

Supply shocks, such as conflicts affecting oil flows, can push prices up even when demand is slowing. That is how stagflation begins, and why a crude spike late in the cycle is a warning, not a sign of strength.
Practice

body.title: Name the Ratio
body.textWithBlank: A capital goods company's new orders divided by its revenue for the same period is called the ___ ratio.
body.explanation: The book-to-bill ratio shows whether the order backlog is growing (above 1) or shrinking (below 1). It is one of the best early reads on the capex cycle at company level.

body.title: Same Sector, Opposite Reactions
body.question: Brent crude jumps from about US$70 to over US$100 a barrel in a few months, and the government signals it wants to keep retail petrol and diesel prices stable. Which outcome is most likely?
options: All energy stocks benefit equally from higher crude prices
Upstream producers gain on higher realisations, though a windfall tax is possible, while oil marketing companies face margin pressure
Oil marketing companies gain the most because they sell more fuel
Crude prices do not affect Indian energy companies because India imports most of its crude
body.explanation: Upstream producers such as ONGC earn more per barrel, although in 2022 the government imposed a windfall tax to capture part of that gain. Oil marketing companies such as IOC, BPCL, and HPCL buy crude at higher prices but may be unable to raise retail prices, so their margins get squeezed, as in April to September 2022 when they posted a combined loss of ₹21,201 crore. India's 88.7% import dependence makes the oil marketing squeeze more painful, not less.

cards.definition: The total value of contracts a company has won but not yet executed. A measure of revenue visibility.
Order inflow divided by revenue for the same period. Above 1 means the backlog is growing.
Operating profit per tonne of metal sold. Swings sharply with metal prices because costs are largely fixed.
A temporary import duty to protect domestic industry from a sudden surge in imports, such as India's duty on flat steel from April 2025.
A levy on unusually high profits caused by price spikes, such as India's special additional excise duty on domestic crude from July 2022 to December 2024.
The margin an oil marketing company earns on selling fuel. It shrinks or turns negative when crude rises but retail prices are held steady.

body.title: Late Cycle or Still Mid Cycle?
body.scenario: It is September 2026. Brent crude has risen from about US$96 to over US$108 in two weeks. India's largest engineering and construction company has a record order book, up 27% in a year, but analysts note softer margins. Government capex is budgeted to rise to ₹12.22 lakh crore. Manufacturing PMI has cooled to its lowest level in five years while services remain strong, and CPI inflation has risen to a seven-month high of 4.82%. You hold capital goods, metal, and oil marketing stocks.
body.prompt: Using the mid vs late cycle signals from this lesson, how would you assess each of your three sector holdings?
body.modelAnswer: The picture mixes mid cycle strength with late cycle warnings. Capital goods still have strong mid cycle support: a record order book and rising government capex give revenue visibility. But softer margins, rising crude, and cooling manufacturing momentum are the late cycle signs to watch, so check whether input cost inflation is eating into contract margins and whether private orders keep growing. Metals depend heavily on global prices and China; cooling manufacturing PMI and high crude-driven costs argue for checking whether steel prices and spreads are still rising or starting to roll over, and not being lulled by a low P/E on strong recent earnings. Oil marketing companies face the most direct risk: a sharp crude spike with political pressure to keep fuel prices stable is exactly the setup that squeezed their margins in 2022. None of this is a sell signal on its own, but it is a reason to reassess position sizes and to watch the next few months of margins, commodity prices, and RBI commentary closely.

body.text: This lesson is educational. Company names are used only as examples of how different business models respond to the cycle, not as recommendations. Figures such as order books, crude prices, and policy measures are as reported at the time of writing and will change.

points: Capital goods tend to lead in the mid cycle as capex takes off; track order inflows, book-to-bill ratios, order book cover, government capex, and GFCF growth
L&T's order book reached ₹7.79 lakh crore in June 2026, up 27% year on year, while central government capex is budgeted at ₹12.22 lakh crore for FY27
Metal producers are global price takers with high fixed costs: in the example, a 10% move in steel prices moved EBITDA per tonne by 55%
China's record 111.1 million tonnes of steel exports in 2024 pushed India to impose a safeguard duty on flat steel imports from April 2025
Energy splits three ways: upstream producers gain from higher crude, oil marketing companies can be squeezed, and power utilities offer steadier regulated growth
In April to September 2022, frozen fuel prices left IOC, BPCL, and HPCL with a combined loss of ₹21,201 crore, while upstream producers faced a windfall tax
Late cycle traps: low P/E on peak earnings, new capacity arriving as demand cools, rising costs squeezing margins, and policy intervention
